toc.title: 11.5 Matrix Based System of Linear Equations

html:
Group A is 11 marks out of 75 — one seventh of the whole Mathematics paper — and it is decided in about fifteen minutes. It is also the cheapest block of marks on the paper, because every item is a single formula, a single condition or a single one-line calculation, and the same handful of formulae come back year after year. Note one change that is verified on the 2082 paper itself: the eleven MCQs now arrive as a separate booklet, issued 30 minutes after the examination starts, and you write their answers on the same answer sheet. So you will begin with Group B, and Group A will interrupt you. Plan for that.

The real pattern, and the real grid

Paper structure (identical on the verified 2079, 2080, 2081 and 2082 papers and on the CDC Model Question-2080):

Group Questions Marks Printed as
A — multiple choice 11 (Q1–Q11) 1 each 11x1=11
B — short answer 8 (Q12–Q19) 5 each 8x5=40
C — long answer 3 (Q20–Q22) 8 each 3x8=24
Total 22 75 Time 3 hrs

There are exactly two "Or" choices in the whole paper, always at Q11 and at Q19. Group C never carries an "Or". Everything else is compulsory.

CDC Specification Grid 2078 — area-wise marks and MCQ counts:

Content area Area-wise marks MCQs
Algebra 20 2
Trigonometry 6 3 shared
Analytic Geometry 9 (across these
Vector 6 three areas)
Statistics & Probability 6 1
Calculus 22 4
Computational Methods or Mechanics 6 1
Total 75 11

Correct a common error now. The bracketed numbers printed beside each area in the syllabus — Algebra 44, Trigonometry 12, Analytic Geometry 20, Vectors 12, Statistics & Probability 12, Calculus 48, Computational Methods/Mechanics 12, adding to 160 — are working hours, not marks. Many students and many coaching sheets quote them as marks. They cannot be marks: the paper is 75. The marks column is the one in the table above.

The grid's own footnote, verbatim: "At least one multiple choice question should be asked from each area (Trigonometry, Analytic geometry and Vector)." That single sentence is why a Trigonometry MCQ is effectively guaranteed every year, even though Trigonometry is only 6 of the 75 marks.

A second printed note is worth knowing: "Questions should be prepared by giving the context and one question may have more than one sub-questions." That is why Group B items arrive as a table, a figure or a stated theorem followed by five one-mark probes.

This chapter is 216 multiple-choice questions, one section per syllabus unit, in syllabus order. Every question carrying a year tag — (NEB 2079), (NEB 2080), (NEB 2081), (NEB 2082), (CDC model 2080) — is a real item from that paper, transcribed from the scan. Untagged questions were written for this book in the same style. Every numerical answer in every key was recomputed with a computer algebra system before printing.

11.1 Permutation and Combination

Of the two Algebra MCQs, one has come from this unit in 2081 and again in 2082. Both times it was pure recall: a counting principle or the relation between P and C. Nothing here needs more than one line of arithmetic.

Result Formula / condition
Basic counting principle m ways then n ways gives m \times n ways
Arrangements, all different P(n,r) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}
Selections, all different C(n,r) = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}
Link between them C(n,r) \times r! = P(n,r)
Arrangements, not all different \frac{n!}{p!\,q!\,r!} for repeats p,q,r
Repetition allowed, r places n^{r}
Circular arrangement of n (n-1)!
Garland / necklace of n \frac{(n-1)!}{2} (clockwise = anticlockwise)
Symmetry of combination C(n,r) = C(n, n-r)
Pascal's rule C(n,r) + C(n,r-1) = C(n+1,r)
Total subsets \sum_{r=0}^{n} C(n,r) = 2^{n}
At least one chosen 2^{n} - 1
Diagonals of an n-gon C(n,2) - n
Boundary values C(n,0) = C(n,n) = 1, P(n,0)=1

Multiple choice questions

  1. Which one is the relation between permutation and combination of n things taken r things at a time? (NEB 2082) [1]aC(n,r) = r!\times P(n,r)bC(n,r)\times r! = P(n,r)cC(n,r)\times r = P(n,r)dC(n,r) = P(n,r)\times r
  2. How many numbers are there in between 999 and 10{,}000? (NEB 2081) [1]a9\times 10^{3}b8\times 10^{3}c9^{4}d8^{4}
  3. The value of P(5,3) is [1]a10b20c60d120
  4. The value of C(10,8) is [1]a45b80c90d360
  5. If C(n,2) = 15 then n equals [1]a5b6c7d15
  6. Five people are to be seated around a round table. The number of arrangements is [1]a5b20c24d120
  7. The number of distinct arrangements of the letters of the word COMMITTEE is [1]a362880b181440c90720d45360
  8. The number of diagonals of a regular decagon is [1]a10b35c45d90
  9. If C(n,8) = C(n,12) then n equals [1]a4b12c20d96
  10. How many three-digit numbers, with no digit repeated, can be formed from the digits 2,3,4,5,6,7? [1]a18b20c120d216
  11. A cricket team of 11 players is to be chosen from 15. The number of ways is [1]a165b455c1365d32760
  12. The number of different garlands that can be made from 8 distinct flowers is [1]a5040b2520c40320d20160
Answer key — 11.1

1. (b) — C(n,r) counts selections; multiplying by r! orders each selection, which is exactly P(n,r).

2. (a) — the numbers strictly between are 1000 to 9999, i.e. all four-digit numbers: 9999-1000+1 = 9000 = 9\times10^{3}.

3. (c) — P(5,3) = 5\times4\times3 = 60.

4. (a) — C(10,8) = C(10,2) = \frac{10\times9}{2} = 45.

5. (b) — \frac{n(n-1)}{2}=15 \Rightarrow n^{2}-n-30=0 \Rightarrow n=6 (the root -5 is rejected).

6. (c) — circular arrangement of n objects is (n-1)! = 4! = 24.

7. (d) — 9 letters with M, T, E each twice: \frac{9!}{2!\,2!\,2!} = \frac{362880}{8} = 45360.

8. (b) — C(10,2) - 10 = 45-10 = 35; the 10 subtracted are the sides.

9. (c) — C(n,r)=C(n,s) with r \ne s forces r+s=n, so n = 8+12 = 20.

10. (c) — 6\times5\times4 = 120, i.e. P(6,3).

11. (c) — C(15,11) = C(15,4) = \frac{15\times14\times13\times12}{24} = 1365.

12. (b) — a garland can be flipped, so \frac{(8-1)!}{2} = \frac{5040}{2} = 2520.

Distractor analysis — Permutation and Combination

Reading C(n,r)\times r! = P(n,r) backwards. This is the exact trap in the 2082 MCQ 1. Option (a), C(n,r) = r!\times P(n,r), is the same equation with the r! on the wrong side. Fix it by size: for n=5, r=3 we have C=10 and P=60, so P is the bigger number, so r! multiplies C, never P.

Order-blindness. In Q11 the distractor 32760 is P(15,4): the student selected and ordered eleven players. A team is a selection. If swapping two chosen objects gives the same answer, use C.

Forgetting the circle costs one factor. In Q6 the distractor 120 = 5! is the answer for a straight bench. Around a table, one person's seat is only relative, so divide by n: (n-1)!.

Forgetting that a garland flips. In Q12 the distractor 5040 = 7! is the circular count. A garland (or necklace) read clockwise equals the same garland read anticlockwise, so halve it.

Counting the sides as diagonals. In Q8 the distractor 45 is C(10,2), the number of all lines joining two vertices. Ten of those are sides.

11.2 Binomial Theorem

Worth reading carefully, because of a fact the four verified papers make plain: Binomial Theorem has never appeared as an MCQ in 2079, 2080, 2081 or 2082. It appears every year, but in Group B (2079 Q12, 2080 Q13b, 2081 Q12, 2082 Q12a) and Group C (2081 Q20a, 2082 Q20a). Learn the facts below for Group B; do not spend Group A revision time here beyond one pass.

Result Formula / condition
Expansion, positive integral index (a+b)^{n} = \sum_{r=0}^{n} C(n,r)\,a^{n-r}b^{r}
General term T_{r+1} = C(n,r)\,a^{n-r}b^{r}
Number of terms n+1
Middle term, n even one term, the \left(\frac{n}{2}+1\right)th
Middle terms, n odd two, the \frac{n+1}{2}th and \frac{n+3}{2}th
Sum of all coefficients (1+x)^{n} at x=1 gives 2^{n}
Any index (1+x)^{n} valid only for |x|<1, infinitely many terms
Euler's number e = 1+\frac{1}{1!}+\frac{1}{2!}+\frac{1}{3!}+\cdots, 2<e<3
Exponential series e^{x} = 1+\frac{x}{1!}+\frac{x^{2}}{2!}+\frac{x^{3}}{3!}+\cdots
General exponential a^{x} = 1 + x\log a + \frac{(x\log a)^{2}}{2!}+\cdots
Logarithmic series \log_e(1+x) = x-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{x^{3}}{3}-\cdots
Its validity -1 < x \leq 1
Other logarithmic series \log_e(1-x) = -x-\frac{x^{2}}{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{3}-\cdots, |x|<1
Approximation for small x, (1+x)^{n} \approx 1+nx

Multiple choice questions

  1. The number of terms in the expansion of (2x+3y)^{12} is [1]a11b12c13d24
  2. In the expansion of (a+b)^{10}, the middle term is the [1]a5thb6thc7thd5th and 6th
  3. The middle term of (2+3x)^{30} is the [1]a15thb16thc17thd15th and 16th
  4. The coefficient of x^{5} in (1+x)^{10} is [1]a120b210c252d504
  5. The sum of the binomial coefficients in the expansion of (1+x)^{n} is [1]anbn!c2^{n}d2^{n}-1
  6. In (1+x)^{11} the coefficients of x^{r} and x^{r+1} are equal. Then r is [1]a4b5c6d11
  7. The expansion of \log_e(1+x) is valid for [1]aall xbx>0c-1 < x \leq 1dx \geq 1
  8. Euler's number e is the sum of the series [1]a\sum \frac{1}{n}b\sum \frac{1}{n!}c\sum \frac{1}{n^{2}}d\sum \frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}
  9. The coefficient of x^{3} in the expansion of e^{2x} is [1]a\frac{1}{6}b\frac{2}{3}c\frac{4}{3}d8
  10. Using the binomial expansion, (1.01)^{5} correct to three decimal places is [1]a1.005b1.050c1.051d1.105
  11. The term independent of x in the expansion of \left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{6} is [1]a15b20c30d64
  12. The number of terms in the expansion of (1+x)^{-3}, |x|<1, is [1]a2b3c4dinfinitely many
Answer key — 11.2

1. (c) — a positive integral index n gives n+1 terms, so 12+1=13.

2. (b) — n=10 is even, so there is one middle term, the \left(\frac{10}{2}+1\right)th =6th.

3. (b) — n=30 is even: the \left(\frac{30}{2}+1\right)th =16th term.

4. (c) — C(10,5) = 252.

5. (c) — put x=1: \sum C(n,r) = (1+1)^{n} = 2^{n}.

6. (b) — C(11,r) = C(11,r+1) needs r+(r+1) = 11, so r=5.

7. (c) — the series diverges at x=-1 and for |x|>1; it converges at x=+1 (giving \log 2).

8. (b) — e = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!} = 1+1+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{6}+\cdots

9. (c) — e^{2x} = \sum \frac{(2x)^{n}}{n!}, so the x^{3} coefficient is \frac{2^{3}}{3!} = \frac{8}{6} = \frac{4}{3}.

10. (c) — (1+0.01)^{5} = 1+5(0.01)+10(0.0001)+\cdots = 1.05101\ldots \approx 1.051.

11. (b) — T_{r+1} = C(6,r)x^{6-2r}; 6-2r=0 gives r=3 and C(6,3)=20.

12. (d) — for a negative (or fractional) index the expansion is an infinite series; it only terminates for a positive integral index.

Distractor analysis — Binomial Theorem

Counting terms as n instead of n+1. Option (b) in Q1 is the commonest wrong answer. The powers of y run 0,1,2,\ldots,12 — thirteen values.

Confusing "rth term" with "coefficient of x^{r}". T_{r+1} carries x^{r}. In Q4 the answer is C(10,5), not C(10,4); the distractor 210 = C(10,4) is exactly the off-by-one.

Applying the "two middle terms" rule to an even index. In Q2 and Q3 the distractor "(d) two middle terms" is the n odd case. Even n gives one middle term. Count the terms first: 11 terms has a 6th in the middle, 31 terms has a 16th.

Ignoring the validity condition. In Q7 and Q12, option (a) "all x" treats a power series as if it were a polynomial. The general binomial theorem and the logarithmic series are only valid on a restricted interval, and the examiner asks for that interval (2081 Q12c did, for 1 mark).

11.3 Complex Numbers

This unit has supplied an Algebra MCQ twice in four years: 2079 asked for a property of the cube roots of unity, 2081 for the polar form of a product. Both are one-line recall. De Moivre's theorem itself has appeared every year, but in Group B or C.

Result Formula / condition
Polar (modulus–amplitude) form z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)
Modulus r = |z| = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}
Argument \theta = \tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x}, placed in the correct quadrant
Product in polar form z_1z_2 = r_1r_2\left[\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)+i\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\right]
Quotient in polar form moduli divide, arguments subtract
De Moivre's theorem \left[r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\right]^{n} = r^{n}(\cos n\theta + i \sin n\theta)
Euler's formula e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta, so e^{i\pi} = -1
Cube roots of unity 1,\ \omega,\ \omega^{2} with \omega = \frac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}
Their sum 1+\omega+\omega^{2} = 0
Their product 1\cdot\omega\cdot\omega^{2} = \omega^{3} = 1
Useful consequence \omega+\omega^{2} = -1 and (1+\omega)(1+\omega^{2}) = 1
nth roots of unity n distinct values, and they sum to 0
Powers of i i^{4k}=1, i^{4k+1}=i, i^{4k+2}=-1, i^{4k+3}=-i
Conjugate z\bar{z} = |z|^{2}

Multiple choice questions

  1. The property of cube roots of unity where \omega is the cube root of unity is (NEB 2079) [1]a1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0b\omega^{3}+1=0c\omega = -\omega^{2}d\omega+\omega^{2}=1
  2. It is given that (r_1,\theta_1) and (r_2,\theta_2) are polar co-ordinates of z_1 and z_2. What are the polar co-ordinates of the image of z_1z_2? (NEB 2081) [1]a(r_1r_2,\ \theta_1-\theta_2)b(r_1r_2,\ \theta_1+\theta_2)c(r_1+r_2,\ \theta_1+\theta_2)d(r_1-r_2,\ \theta_1+\theta_2)
  3. The modulus of 1+i\sqrt{3} is [1]a1b\sqrt{2}c2d4
  4. The argument of -1+i is [1]a\frac{\pi}{4}b\frac{3\pi}{4}c-\frac{\pi}{4}d\frac{5\pi}{4}
  5. If \omega is a complex cube root of unity, then \omega^{10}+\omega^{11} equals [1]a0b1c-1d\omega
  6. If \omega is a complex cube root of unity, then (1+\omega)(1+\omega^{2}) equals [1]a-1b0c1d2
  7. By De Moivre's theorem, (\cos 20^{\circ}+i\sin 20^{\circ})^{9} equals [1]a1b-1cid-i
  8. The value of e^{i\pi/2} is [1]a1b-1cid-i
  9. The number of distinct fifth roots of unity is [1]a1b2c5dinfinitely many
  10. The polar form of 1+i is [1]a\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)b2\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)c\sqrt{2}\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{3}\right)d\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}
  11. The value of i^{37} is [1]a1b-1cid-i
  12. The sum of all the fifth roots of unity is [1]a0b1c5d-1
Answer key — 11.3

1. (a) — \omega satisfies \omega^{3}=1, i.e. (\omega-1)(\omega^{2}+\omega+1)=0; since \omega \ne 1, 1+\omega+\omega^{2}=0.

2. (b) — multiplying complex numbers multiplies the moduli and adds the arguments.

3. (c) — \sqrt{1^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}} = \sqrt{4} = 2.

4. (b) — the point (-1,1) is in the second quadrant, so \theta = \pi - \frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{3\pi}{4}.

5. (c) — \omega^{10}=\omega^{9}\cdot\omega=\omega and \omega^{11}=\omega^{2}, so the sum is \omega+\omega^{2}=-1.

6. (c) — expand: 1+\omega+\omega^{2}+\omega^{3} = 0 + 1 = 1.

7. (b) — \cos 180^{\circ}+i\sin 180^{\circ} = -1; machine-checked.

8. (c) — \cos\frac{\pi}{2}+i\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 0+i = i.

9. (c) — the equation z^{5}=1 has exactly 5 distinct roots.

10. (a) — r=\sqrt{2} and \theta = \tan^{-1}1 = \frac{\pi}{4} (first quadrant).

11. (c) — 37 = 4(9)+1, so i^{37}=i^{1}=i.

12. (a) — the roots of z^{5}-1=0 sum to minus the coefficient of z^{4}, which is 0.

Distractor analysis — Complex Numbers

Writing \omega^{3}+1=0 instead of \omega^{3}-1=0. Option (b) in the 2079 MCQ 1 is the cube root of -1, not of 1. Anchor it on the real root: \omega=1 must satisfy the equation, and 1^{3}-1=0.

Losing the quadrant when finding an argument. In Q4, \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{-1} = -\frac{\pi}{4} comes straight off a calculator, and it is option (c) — the wrong answer, because (-1,1) is in the second quadrant. Always plot the point first.

Adding the moduli. Option (c) in the 2081 MCQ, (r_1+r_2,\theta_1+\theta_2), treats multiplication as addition in the modulus. Moduli multiply; only arguments add.

Forgetting to reduce the power modulo 3 (or 4). In Q5 and Q11 a student who tries to compute \omega^{10} directly loses time and accuracy. Use \omega^{3}=1 and i^{4}=1 to knock the exponent down first.

11.4 Sequence and Series

This unit is examined as a single-line recall MCQ or, far more often, as mathematical induction in Group B/C — induction appears in every verified year (2079 Q13a, 2080 Q20b, 2081 Q20c, 2082 Q20b, CDC model Q20c). Memorise the three sum formulae exactly; every mark here hangs on them.

Result Formula
Sum of first n natural numbers \sum n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}
Sum of their squares \sum n^{2} = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}
Sum of their cubes \sum n^{3} = \left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^{2}
A useful identity \sum n^{3} = \left(\sum n\right)^{2}
Sum of first n odd numbers 1+3+5+\cdots+(2n-1) = n^{2}
Sum of first n even numbers 2+4+6+\cdots+2n = n(n+1)
Induction, step 1 verify the statement for n=1 (the base case)
Induction, step 2 assume it true for n=k (the inductive hypothesis)
Induction, step 3 prove it for n=k+1 using that assumption
Induction, conclusion true for all n \in \mathbb{N}

Multiple choice questions

  1. The sum of the first 5 odd natural numbers is (CDC model 2080) [1]a15b20c25d30
  2. The value of 1^{2}+2^{2}+3^{2}+\cdots+20^{2} is [1]a2470b2870c3080d4410
  3. The value of 1^{3}+2^{3}+3^{3}+\cdots+10^{3} is [1]a385b1000c3025d3850
  4. The value of 1+2+3+\cdots+100 is [1]a4950b5000c5050d10100
  5. The sum of the first n even natural numbers is [1]an^{2}bn(n+1)c\frac{n(n+1)}{2}d2n
  6. 1^{2}+2^{2}+\cdots+n^{2} equals [1]a\frac{n(n+1)}{2}b\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}c\left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^{2}d\frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}
  7. Which statement is true for every positive integer n? [1]a\sum n^{2} = \left(\sum n\right)^{2}b\sum n^{3} = \left(\sum n\right)^{2}c\sum n^{3} = \left(\sum n^{2}\right)^{2}d\sum n = \left(\sum n^{2}\right)^{2}
  8. In a proof by mathematical induction, the first thing you must do is [1]aassume the result for n=kbverify the result for the smallest ncprove the result for n=k+1ddifferentiate both sides
  9. The value of 1^{2}+2^{2}+\cdots+6^{2} is [1]a36b49c91d441
  10. The sum of the cubes of the first 5 natural numbers is [1]a125b225c325d625
Answer key — 11.4

1. (c) — 1+3+5+7+9=25, which is 5^{2}: the sum of the first n odd numbers is n^{2}.

2. (b) — \frac{20\times21\times41}{6} = 2870.

3. (c) — \left[\frac{10\times11}{2}\right]^{2} = 55^{2} = 3025.

4. (c) — \frac{100\times101}{2} = 5050.

5. (b) — 2(1+2+\cdots+n) = 2\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2} = n(n+1).

6. (b) — the standard result; (c) is the sum of cubes.

7. (b) — the sum of cubes is the square of the sum of the first powers, e.g. 1+8+27=36=6^{2}.

8. (b) — the base case. Without it the inductive step proves nothing.

9. (c) — \frac{6\times7\times13}{6} = 91.

10. (b) — \left[\frac{5\times6}{2}\right]^{2} = 15^{2} = 225.

Distractor analysis — Sequence and Series

Swapping \sum n^{2} and \sum n^{3}. These two formulae are adjacent in memory and are the most-swapped pair in the whole Algebra area. Check with n=2: \sum n^{2} = 5 and \sum n^{3} = 9. Feed n=2 into a formula you are unsure of and see which number comes out.

n^{2} versus n(n+1) for the odd/even sums. Q1 and Q5 pair these deliberately. Odd numbers start at 1 and sum to n^{2}; even numbers start at 2 and sum to n(n+1), which is exactly twice \sum n.

Skipping the base case in induction. Option (a) in Q8 is what most scripts actually do first, and it loses the mark the grid allocates to it. The 2081 paper asked candidates to state the principle of mathematical induction for 2 marks — both the base case and the inductive step must appear in words.

Off-by-one in \sum n for a range. For "the sum of the integers from 1 to 100", 4950 (option (a) in Q4) is \sum_{1}^{99}. Substitute the top limit itself, not one less.

11.5 Matrix Based System of Linear Equations

The 2082 paper put Cramer's rule straight into Group A (MCQ 2), and Group C has carried a full matrix-method system in 2079, 2080 and 2082. Learn the three methods as three different tools for the same job, and learn the consistency conditions — they are what the MCQ actually tests.

Result Formula / condition
Matrix form of a system AX = B
Cramer's rule x=\frac{D_x}{D}, y=\frac{D_y}{D}, z=\frac{D_z}{D}
D_x replace the x-column of D by the constants
Unique solution D \ne 0
No solution (inconsistent) D=0 but some D_x, D_y, D_z \ne 0
Infinitely many solutions D = 0 and D_x=D_y=D_z=0
Inverse matrix method X = A^{-1}B, valid only if |A| \ne 0
The inverse itself A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\,\mathrm{adj}\,A
2\times2 inverse rule swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by |A|
Singular matrix |A| = 0, so A^{-1} does not exist
Determinant of the adjoint |\mathrm{adj}\,A| = |A|^{n-1}
Determinant of the inverse |A^{-1}| = \frac{1}{|A|}
Row-equivalent (Gauss) method row-operate the augmented matrix to upper triangular form, then back-substitute
Augmented matrix the coefficient matrix with the constant column attached

For a two-variable system, Cramer's rule is three determinants and one division. Draw them out before you substitute — that alone prevents most sign errors.

So x = \dfrac{D_x}{D} and y = \dfrac{D_y}{D} — written out,

y = \frac{p_1r_2-p_2r_1}{p_1q_2-p_2q_1}

The row-equivalent method works on the augmented matrix instead. One row operation at a time, and you write the operation beside the row you changed.

Multiple choice questions

  1. If the system of equations is p_1x+q_1y=r_1 and p_2x+q_2y=r_2, what is the value of y? (NEB 2082) [1]a\frac{r_1q_2-r_2q_1}{p_1q_2-p_2q_1}b\frac{p_1r_2-p_2r_1}{p_1q_2-p_2q_1}c\frac{p_1q_2-p_2q_1}{p_1r_2-p_2r_1}d\frac{p_2r_1-p_1r_2}{p_1q_2-p_2q_1}
  2. A system of linear equations has a unique solution if and only if [1]aD=0bD \ne 0cD_x = 0dD=D_x=D_y=0
  3. If A has first row (2,\ 3) and second row (3,\ -1), then |A| equals [1]a-11b-7c7d11

The sign error in the cross product. Three separate things must be kept straight, and the papers test all three.

  • The \hat{j} component carries a minus. Expanding a 3\times3 determinant, the middle term is subtracted: \vec{a}\times\vec{b} = (a_2b_3-a_3b_2)\hat{i} - (a_1b_3-a_3b_1)\hat{j} + (a_1b_2-a_2b_1)\hat{k}. Dropping that minus is the commonest single error in the whole Vector area.
  • The cross product is anti-commutative but the dot product is not. \vec{a}\times\vec{b} = -(\vec{b}\times\vec{a}), while \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b} = \vec{b}\cdot\vec{a}. Order matters for one and not the other.
  • The cyclic order. \hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}, \hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i}, \hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j} — going forwards round the circle. Going backwards flips the sign. Option (b) is the trap, and it is the most-chosen wrong answer on that paper.

Treating (\vec{a}-\vec{b})\times(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) like a difference of squares. Options (b) and (d) in the 2079 item are |\vec{a}|^{2}-|\vec{b}|^{2}, which is what (\vec{a}-\vec{b})\cdot(\vec{a}+\vec{b}) gives. A cross product cannot produce a scalar. Check the type of the answer before the value.

Distractor analysis — Derivatives

Circular versus hyperbolic derivatives. \frac{d}{dx}(\cos x)=-\sin x but \frac{d}{dx}(\cosh x)=+\sinh x. The hyperbolic pair has no minus sign; the circular pair does. The minus signs in the hyperbolic family belong to \coth, \mathrm{sech}, \mathrm{cosech} and to the two inverse functions \mathrm{sech}^{-1}, \mathrm{cosech}^{-1} — nowhere else.

Inverse circular versus inverse hyperbolic. The three most-confused pairs are \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}} (for \sin^{-1}) against \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}} (for \sinh^{-1}); \frac{1}{1+x^{2}} (for \tan^{-1}) against \frac{1}{1-x^{2}} (for \tanh^{-1}); and \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^{2}-1}} (for \cosh^{-1}), which has no circular twin at all. Distractor analysis — Anti-derivatives

Differentiating when the question said integrate — and the reverse. This is the most expensive single confusion in the Calculus area, and both directions appear as distractors. In question 18, option (c) a^{x}\log a is the derivative of a^{x} offered as its integral. In question 6, option (a) \sec^{2}x is the derivative of \tan x. In question 16, option (d) \sinh x has done nothing at all. Two habits fix it: (i) underline the word "integral" or "derivative" in the stem before reading the options; (ii) differentiate your chosen option and check it gives back the integrand — for a one-mark MCQ this takes ten seconds and is completely reliable.

\frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{a} written as \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{a}{x}. The 2081 MCQ 8 offers exactly this as option (a). The argument of \tan^{-1} must be \frac{x}{a} — the variable on top. The misplaced constant in \int\frac{dx}{9x^{2}+1}. The 2082 MCQ 8 offers \frac{1}{27} three times over. Do it in two clean steps. First factor: \frac{1}{9}\int\frac{dx}{x^{2}+\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}}. Then apply the formula with a=\frac{1}{3}: \frac{1}{9}\times 3 = \frac{1}{3}. An anomaly worth knowing about

Distractor analysis — Computational Methods

Subtracting in the wrong direction. In both real elimination MCQs an option carries the correct coefficient with the wrong sign — question 2's option (d) is -10y=10. Write the operation on the paper exactly as the question states it (R_2 \to 2R_1-R_2 means first row doubled minus second row, not the reverse) and do the constants in the same order as the coefficients.

Doubling the coefficients but forgetting the constant. Option (b) 10y=18 in question 2 comes from doubling only the left side of R_1. The row operation acts on the whole row of the augmented matrix, constant column included. This is why §11.5's augmented-matrix figure keeps the constants inside the bracket.

"Inconsistent with infinitely many solutions." The 2079 option (c) is a sentence that cannot be true: inconsistent means no solution. Read all four options before choosing; the examiner is testing whether you know the vocabulary, not the arithmetic.

Confusing the pivot column rule with the pivot row rule. Question 11's option (d) "the smallest ratio" is the rule for the departing variable (the pivot row), not the entering one. Column first by the most negative objective entry, then row by the smallest non-negative ratio.

Treating rank alone as decisive. Rank of the coefficient matrix on its own tells you nothing: it must be compared with the rank of the augmented matrix, and then both with n. Three quantities, two comparisons.

Distractor analysis — Mechanics

Time of flight halved. Question 5's option (a), 2 s, is \frac{u\sin\theta}{g} — the time to the greatest height, which is half the time of flight. The 2082 stem gives you the same u and \theta as the height question above it, so the two are easy to answer in one breath and equally easy to mix up: t_{\text{top}}=\frac{u\sin\theta}{g}=2 s, T=4 s.

Halving in the wrong place. In the 2081 item, u^{2}=25600 and \sin^{2}30^\circ=\frac14; option (d) 640 m is what you get from \frac{u^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}{g}, forgetting the 2 in the denominator, and option (a) 203 m is a decimal-slip distractor. Squaring the sine, or not. In the 2082 item, option (b) 40 m is \frac{u^{2}\sin\theta}{2g} — the sine used un-squared. H carries \sin^{2}\theta; R carries \sin 2\theta. These are different functions and the options are built to punish swapping them: \sin^{2}30^\circ=0.25 but \sin 60^\circ\approx0.866.

Dropping g from a weight. The 2080 item's option (a), "100 newtons", treats kilograms as newtons. Mass is in kilograms; weight is the force mg in newtons. The examiner left g symbolic precisely so that you could not hide behind a number.

Force confused with change of momentum. The 2079 item's printed options all divide by t, which makes them all forces. Impulse =Ft=mv-mu is the change of momentum; \frac{mv-mu}{t} is the average force. Know both relations and you can still pick the intended option, (b), while recognising that the question stem does not match its options.

Force ratio read the right way round. In question 10, the resultant of two like parallel forces sits closer to the bigger force, so AP:PB = Y:X, the inverse of the force ratio. Test it with X=3, Y=1: the resultant should be a quarter of the way from A, and Y:X=1:3 gives exactly that.

11.17 Appendix: Retained Examinable Topics

A few topics sit outside the fifteen numbered units of the Grade 12 spine but have still appeared as Group A questions. They are collected here so that you can see exactly how much time each deserves, rather than guessing.

Group Theory. An MCQ in 2079 (recognising an abelian group) and again in 2080 (naming the associative law for a binary operation) — and then absent from both 2081 and 2082. The 2078 specification grid has no line for it. Treat it as a fifteen-minute revision: learn the four group axioms and the word "abelian", and move on. Do not learn subgroups, cosets or cyclic groups for this paper.

Rolle's theorem and the Mean Value Theorem. Appeared in 2080 only, and not in 2079, 2081 or 2082. Learn the two statements and the difference between them — that is the whole examinable surface.

Numerical integration (trapezoidal and Simpson's rules). Not seen as an MCQ in any of the four verified years, but the formulae are short and they occasionally appear inside a Group B part. Ten minutes.

Sum and product of the roots of a quadratic. A Grade 11 result, but it was MCQ 2 in 2080. It costs one line to remember.

Distractor analysis — retained topics

Answering with a root instead of the sum. In the real 2080 item the roots of x^{2}-6x+8=0 are 2 and 4, and both appear as options, as does the product 8. Use -\frac{b}{a} and \frac{c}{a} directly; do not solve the quadratic at all — solving is what makes you reach for the wrong number.

Sign lost from -\frac{b}{a}. The sum of the roots is -\frac{b}{a}, not \frac{b}{a}. With b=-6 the two differ only in sign, and in a paper where the answer happens to be positive the mistake goes unnoticed until the year it does not.

Confusing the group axioms by name. The 2080 item prints all four axiom names as options. Memorise them as a sentence: closure keeps you in the set, associativity moves the brackets, identity does nothing, inverse undoes. Commutativity is the extra one that makes a group abelian — it is not one of the four.

Calling (\mathbb{N},+) a group. It is closed and associative but has no identity element (0\notin\mathbb{N}) and no inverses. This is option (b) in the 2079 item and it is the one most often chosen.

Rolle answered with an endpoint. In question 4, options (a) and (c) are a and b themselves. Rolle's theorem promises a c strictly inside (a,b); an endpoint can never be the answer.

Trapezoidal answer replaced by the exact value. In question 8, option (a) \frac13 is \int_0^1 x^2dx done exactly. The question asks what the rule produces, which is deliberately not the exact value — that gap is the whole point of an error estimate.

Chapter summary

  • Group A is eleven marks in fifteen minutes, and since 2082 it arrives as a separate booklet thirty minutes after the paper starts. Do the eleven MCQs first, in one pass, and hand the booklet back before you settle into Group B.
  • Four of the eleven MCQs are Calculus — the single largest block. Across 2079–2082 the reliable slots have been a derivative (often an inverse hyperbolic or inverse trigonometric one), a standard integral of the \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{a} family, and one or two differential-equation items on order/degree, homogeneity or the integrating factor.
  • One MCQ is guaranteed from each of Trigonometry, Analytic Geometry and Vector by the grid's own footnote. In practice that has meant a half-angle or triangle law, a conic property (eccentricity, latus rectum or a tangency condition), and a dot- or cross-product item.
  • One MCQ is guaranteed from Computational Methods or Mechanics, and three of the four verified years made it a Gauss-elimination row-operation step; the Mechanics alternative has twice been the greatest height of a projectile. Both are pure substitution.
  • The Statistics and Probability MCQ has gone to Probability every single year, never to correlation or regression, and conditional probability has appeared in 2080, 2081, 2082 and the CDC model. P(B/A)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)} — divide by the event that has already happened.
  • Exactly two "Or" choices appear per paper, at Q11 and Q19, never in Group C. Decide in advance which branch you are taking so that you do not spend reading time on both.
  • The traps that cost the most marks are, in order of how often they are printed: differentiating when asked to integrate; the \hat{j} sign and the non-commutativity of \vec{a}\times\vec{b}; \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{a}{x} written for \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{a}, and the constant misplaced in \int\frac{dx}{9x^{2}+1}; dividing by P(B) instead of P(A) in a conditional probability; degree read as order; C(n,r)\times r! = P(n,r) read backwards; and c^{2}=a^{2}(1+m^{2}) with a and c swapped.
  • Binomial Theorem and Solution of Triangles have never carried an MCQ in the four verified years, and Group Theory vanished after 2080 while Rolle/MVT appeared in 2080 only. Prepare them for Groups B and C, not for Group A.
  • Every numerical answer key in this chapter was recomputed with a computer algebra system before it was printed, including the option sets of the real past papers — where three genuine printing faults were found and are flagged in place.
How to attack Group A in fifteen minutes

Minutes 0–1: sort, do not solve. Read all eleven stems once and mark each one recall, one-line, or work. Roughly half of any NEB Group A is pure recall — order and degree, a group axiom, Lami's theorem, the exactness condition, the pivot rule.

Minutes 1–6: clear every recall item. Answer them straight off the fact tables in this chapter. Do not check them twice; you either know a definition or you do not.

Minutes 6–12: the one-line items. These are the substitution questions — greatest height, an integrating factor, a conditional probability, a row operation, an eccentricity. Write the formula down before you write any number. Nearly every distractor in this book is generated by substituting into a half-remembered formula, so the formula on the page is your defence.

Minutes 12–15: the work items and a sweep. Usually one or two: a determinant, a cross product, a definite integral. Then sweep the whole sheet and confirm you have shaded exactly eleven bubbles.

Three habits worth more than any formula. (i) Read the operator. "Find \int…" versus "find \frac{d}{dx}…" and "\hat{k}\times\hat{j}" versus "\hat{j}\times\hat{k}" change the sign or invert the whole answer. (ii) Check the variable. Differentiate with respect to whatever the question names, not whatever letter is most prominent. (iii) Never leave a blank. There is no negative marking; eliminate the two options that are dimensionally or structurally impossible and choose between the rest.
